title: Knight Hops to a Square
statement:
A chess knight stands on square (0, 0) of a board that goes on forever in every direction. In one hop it moves two squares along one axis and one square along the other, so from (x, y) it can reach the eight squares (x ± 1, y ± 2) and (x ± 2, y ± 1).

Return the smallest number of hops that brings the knight to square (x, y). Every square can be reached.

examples.why: The square right next door is far for a knight: for example (0, 0) → (2, 1) → (0, 2) → (1, 0). No route of 1 or 2 hops lands there.

The answer is the same as for (2, 2), its mirror image. That square looks close but is awkward: no 2-hop route lands on it, and 3 hops are impossible because every hop changes x + y by an odd amount. So it takes 4.

hints: Each hop is one edge in a graph whose nodes are squares. Which search finds the fewest edges?
The board is symmetric: the answer for (x, y) is the same as for (|x|, |y|). How does that shrink the search?
Run BFS from the origin toward (|x|, |y|) and only allow squares with both coordinates at least −2. A shortest path never needs to wander further into the negative side than that.

explain.intuition:
Hops all cost the same, so this is a shortest path in an unweighted graph, which is exactly what BFS gives: it visits squares in rings of 1 hop, 2 hops and so on, and the first time it reaches the target is the minimum.

An infinite board needs bounds. Mirror the target into the first quadrant with (|x|, |y|), since the moves are symmetric. A shortest path may step slightly behind the origin, which is why (1, 0) needs a detour, but never more than 2 squares. So BFS over squares with coordinates from −2 up to the target plus 2 is enough. That keeps the search to a few hundred thousand squares at most.
steps: Start BFS from (0, 0) at distance 0 with a visited set.
Pop a square. If it is the target, return its distance.
Push each of the 8 hops that stays within −2 ≤ coord ≤ target + 2 and is not visited yet, at distance + 1.
pitfalls: Forbidding negative coordinates entirely. Then (1, 1) and (1, 0) come out too long or unreachable, because their shortest routes step below zero.
Using a greedy rule like 'hop toward the target until close'. Near the target the greedy choice is wrong, as (1, 0) needing 3 hops shows.
Marking squares visited when popped instead of when pushed. The same square enters the queue many times and the search slows down badly.

complexity.time: O(|x| · |y|) squares in the bounded box

solutions.title: BFS in a bounded box
solutions.idea: Mirror the target into the first quadrant and BFS over squares from −2 to target + 2.

solutions.title: Memoised walk back to the origin
solutions.idea: From (x, y) in the first quadrant, the best first step back is one of the two hops that reduce both coordinates. Mirror after each step and memoise.

followups: Speed it up with BFS from both ends at once. Why does that shrink the explored area?
The board is now finite, n by n, with some squares blocked. Which parts of the solution still apply?
